items.title: Assuming Countable Choice, the integral function of a Riemann-integrable function is Lipschitz and differentiable almost everywhere, with derivative equal to the integrand there
items.strategy: Use the published Lipschitz estimate for the integral function. Lebesgue's criterion makes the discontinuity set of the integrand null under Countable Choice, and the pointwise first FTC gives the derivative at every point outside that set, including the appropriate one-sided endpoint statement.

items.title: Newton–Leibniz needs only continuity on $[a,b]$, differentiability on $(a,b)$, and a Riemann-integrable extension of the interior derivative
items.strategy: For an arbitrary partition, apply the mean value theorem only on its open subintervals. Each endpoint increment lies between the lower and upper Darboux contributions of the given integrable extension; sum, telescope, and squeeze between the lower and upper integrals. The extension's endpoint values are never used.

items.title: Newton–Leibniz remains valid across finitely many exceptional interior points when the primitive is continuous
items.strategy: Order the finite exceptional set, split the interval at those points, apply the interior-derivative Newton–Leibniz theorem on every resulting closed subinterval, and telescope the endpoint differences. Empty exceptional sets and exceptions at the written endpoints reduce to the preceding theorem.

items.title: Integration by parts for continuous factors with Riemann-integrable extensions of their interior derivatives
items.strategy: The product is continuous on the closed interval and differentiable in the interior. The product rule identifies its interior derivative, the algebra of Riemann-integrable functions makes both product terms integrable, and the strengthened Newton–Leibniz theorem evaluates the integral of the product derivative.

items.title: Substitution for a continuous inner map with a Riemann-integrable extension of its interior derivative, without monotonicity or injectivity
items.strategy: Let $F$ be the integral function of the continuous outer integrand. The first FTC and the chain rule identify the interior derivative of $F\circ\varphi$ as $(f\circ\varphi)h$, where $h$ is the integrable derivative extension. Prove that product integrable, apply interior Newton–Leibniz, and retain oriented limits when the two endpoint images reverse or coincide.

items.title: For an integrable $f$, the one-sided derivatives of $F(x)=\int_a^x f$ equal the corresponding one-sided limits of $f$; at a jump they are unequal
items.strategy: Write each one-sided difference quotient as the average of $f$ over the interval between the base point and the varying point. Subtract the relevant one-sided limit and bound the average error by the local supremum error. At an interior point the ordinary derivative exists exactly when the two one-sided limits agree; the value $f(c)$ itself is immaterial unless continuity is asserted.

items.title: Leibniz's rule on a compact rectangle: an interior parameter derivative with a continuous extension may be passed through a Riemann integral
items.strategy: Assume the integrand is continuous on the compact rectangle and its parameter partial derivative exists in the interior parameter range and extends continuously to the rectangle. For an interior parameter increment, apply the one-variable mean value theorem at each fixed integration variable. Uniform continuity of the extension makes the resulting difference quotient converge uniformly to it. The published uniform integral-error bound passes the limit through the Riemann integral; the same estimate gives the relative one-sided endpoint derivatives and continuity of the derivative extension.

items.title: The two FTC forms for a Riemann–Stieltjes integral with a $C^1$ integrator
items.strategy: Reduce every Stieltjes integral on a subinterval to the ordinary integral of $f\alpha'$. The pointwise first FTC gives the derivative of the accumulation function wherever $f$ is continuous. For Newton–Leibniz, apply the interior-derivative theorem to a continuous $G$ whose interior derivative is $f\alpha'$, yielding $\int_a^b f\,d\alpha=G(b)-G(a)$ without endpoint derivatives.

title: The Fundamental Theorems of Calculus: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $G(x)=x^2\sin(1/x)$ has a bounded derivative discontinuous at $0$ that is nevertheless Riemann integrable, and Newton–Leibniz evaluates its integral
items.strategy: Define $G(0)=0$, calculate $G'(0)=0$ from the difference quotient and $G'(x)=2x\sin(1/x)-\cos(1/x)$ away from zero. Bound the derivative, note that its sole discontinuity is at zero, invoke the finite-discontinuity integrability criterion, and apply Newton–Leibniz on $[0,1]$.

items.title: Volterra's function is differentiable everywhere with bounded derivative, but its derivative is not Riemann integrable
items.strategy: Use the published Smith–Volterra–Cantor set. On each complementary interval insert a truncated mirrored copy of $x^2\sin(1/x)$ whose derivative is zero at the joins, and set the function to zero on the fat Cantor set. Prove differentiability with derivative zero on that set and a uniform derivative bound. Every neighborhood of every fat-Cantor point contains derivative values separated by a fixed amount; combine the quantitative positive-measure cover bound with Darboux oscillation to force every upper-minus-lower sum above a positive constant.

items.title: A bounded increasing integrand discontinuous at every rational has an integral function nondifferentiable at every rational in $(0,1)$
items.strategy: Restrict the published prescribed-jump function to $[0,1]`. It is bounded, monotone, and hence Riemann integrable. At each rational interior point its left and right limits exist and differ, so the one-sided FTC gives unequal one-sided derivatives of its integral function. Irrational points remain continuity points and hence differentiability points by the pointwise FTC.

items.title: Thomae's integrand is discontinuous at every rational, yet its integral function is identically zero and differentiable everywhere
items.strategy: Use the published integrability and zero-integral theorem for Thomae's function. Positivity and monotonicity of the integral squeeze every subinterval integral between zero and the full integral, so the accumulation function is identically zero. Its derivative is therefore zero everywhere, agreeing with the integrand at irrationals and differing at every rational.

items.title: The indicator of $\{1,1/2,1/4,1/8,\ldots\}$ is discontinuous at $0$, but its integral function has derivative $0=f(0)$ there
items.strategy: Define the value at zero to be zero. Prove integrability and integral zero by isolating finitely many large spikes in short partition intervals and confining all remaining spikes to a short interval at zero. The integral function is constant zero, while the sequence of spikes proves discontinuity at zero; nevertheless its derivative there equals the chosen value zero.

items.title: The Cantor function is continuous, has derivative $0$ off a null set, and still rises from $0$ to $1$
items.strategy: Use the published facts that the Cantor function is continuous, has endpoint values zero and one, and is locally constant on every component of the complement of the null Cantor set. It follows directly that its derivative is zero at every complementary point, while its endpoint change is one. This isolates why an almost-everywhere derivative hypothesis alone is not the Riemann Newton–Leibniz theorem.

items.title: Paths in $\mathbb{R}^n$, inscribed polygonal sums, arc length as their supremum, and rectifiability
Refining a partition cannot decrease its inscribed polygonal length
items.strategy: It is enough to insert one new partition point. The old chord is no longer than the sum of the two replacement chords by the Euclidean triangle inequality; all other terms agree. Iterate over the finitely many inserted points, including a repeated insertion as a no-op.

items.title: A path in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is rectifiable exactly when every coordinate has bounded variation
items.strategy: For each partition, every scalar coordinate increment is bounded by the Euclidean chord, giving $\operatorname{Var}(\gamma_i)\le L(\gamma)$. Conversely the Euclidean chord is at most the sum of the absolute coordinate increments, so $L(\gamma)\le\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(\gamma_i)$. Take suprema and retain the singleton interval and $n=1$ cases explicitly.

items.title: Arc length is additive across every subdivision point and decreases under restriction
items.strategy: Splice partitions from the two adjacent subintervals to get one inequality. For the other, insert the subdivision point into an arbitrary partition, use refinement monotonicity, and split the resulting finite sum. Treat a subdivision at either endpoint through the zero-length singleton convention.

items.title: Arc length is invariant under every continuous surjective monotone reparametrization, including pauses and reversal
items.strategy: A monotone map sends a partition to an ordered list whose repetitions can be deleted without changing the polygonal sum, proving one inequality. Conversely choose ordered preimages of the finitely many points of any target partition; monotonicity makes them a partition of the source. Apply the same argument to nonincreasing maps after reversing the order, and include constant paths and singleton intervals.

items.title: A $C$-Lipschitz map multiplies path length by at most $C$; isometries preserve length and scalar dilation multiplies it by the absolute scale
items.strategy: Apply the Lipschitz inequality to each chord of each partition and take suprema. Apply the result in both directions for an isometry. For translation and orthogonal maps compute chord norms directly; for scalar dilation use homogeneity, including scale zero and a zero-length path.

items.title: Arc length is lower semicontinuous under uniform convergence of paths
items.strategy: Fix a finite partition. Uniform convergence gives convergence of the finitely many vertices and hence of that polygonal sum. Each approximating sum is bounded by the approximating path's length, so the limiting sum is bounded by the liminf of those lengths. Take the supremum over partitions only after this fixed-partition inequality.

items.title: If $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $\gamma'$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, then $L(\gamma)=\int_a^b\lVert\gamma'(t)\rVert_2\,dt$
items.strategy: Vector Newton–Leibniz and the norm inequality bound every chord sum above by the speed integral. For the reverse bound, use uniform continuity of the extended derivative: on a fine partition, compare each derivative Riemann term with the corresponding chord through the integral of $\gamma'(t)-\gamma'(\xi_i)$, sum the uniform errors, and pass to the Riemann integral. State the endpoint-extension convention and singleton interval separately.

items.title: A continuous piecewise-$C^1$ path is rectifiable and its length is the sum of the speed integrals over its pieces
items.strategy: Choose the finite break partition from the hypothesis. Apply the $C^1$ formula to every restriction using its one-sided endpoint derivative extensions, then add the lengths with subdivision additivity. Corners are allowed because no equality of derivatives across a break is asserted.

items.title: The arc-length function $s_\gamma(t)=L(\gamma|_{[a,t]})$ of a rectifiable path
The arc-length function of a continuous rectifiable path is continuous and nondecreasing, with increments equal to subpath lengths
items.strategy: Additivity gives $s(v)-s(u)=L(\gamma|_{[u,v]})\ge0$. Each coordinate is continuous and BV by the componentwise theorem; the published jump theorem makes each scalar variation function continuous. Bound each subpath length by the sum of its coordinate variations to squeeze the increment of $s$ to zero from either side, including endpoints.

items.title: Every rectifiable path factors through its arc-length function as a unit-speed path on $[0,L]$
items.strategy: Continuity makes the nondecreasing length function onto $[0,L]$. Define the new path by $\bar\gamma(s(t))=\gamma(t)$; if two parameters have the same length value, additivity forces the intervening subpath to have zero length and hence equal endpoints, so this is well defined. Chord distance is at most subpath length, making $\bar\gamma$ $1$-Lipschitz. Use monotone reparametrization and additivity on arbitrary subintervals of $[0,L]$ to prove their lengths equal their parameter differences. Handle $L=0$ as a singleton-domain constant path.

items.title: A regular $C^1$ path has a $C^1$ arc-length reparametrization with derivative of Euclidean norm one
items.strategy: The $C^1$ length formula gives $s(t)=\int_a^t\lVert\gamma'\rVert$ and the pointwise FTC gives $s'=\lVert\gamma'\rVert>0$. Thus $s$ is a strictly increasing continuous bijection. Apply the derivative-of-an-inverse theorem and the chain rule to $\bar\gamma=\gamma\circ s^{-1}$; division by the speed gives derivative norm one. Compactness and positivity make the inverse derivative continuous, including its one-sided endpoint extensions.

title: Arc Length and Rectifiable Curves: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A line segment has length equal to the distance between its endpoints, and a finitely piecewise-linear path has length equal to the sum of its edge lengths
items.strategy: For a line segment every ordered chord is a nonnegative scalar multiple of the same displacement vector, so every polygonal sum telescopes to the endpoint distance. Apply the piecewise-$C^1$ formula or subdivision additivity to a finite vertex list, retaining zero-length edges and repeated vertices.

items.title: The continuous path $\gamma(x)=(x,x\sin(1/x))$ on $[0,1]$, with $\gamma(0)=(0,0)$, is not rectifiable
items.strategy: Choose a decreasing sequence tending to zero where the second coordinate alternates between positive and negative values of harmonic order. Partitions containing the reversed finite initial segment have second-coordinate variation bounded below by a divergent harmonic subseries. Hence that coordinate is not BV, and the componentwise rectifiability theorem makes the path nonrectifiable.

items.title: $\gamma(t)=(t,|t|)$ on $[-1,1]$ is rectifiable of length $2\sqrt{2}$ but is not differentiable at $0$
items.strategy: Split at zero. Each restriction is affine with constant speed $\sqrt2$, so the piecewise-$C^1$ formula gives two contributions of $\sqrt2$. The left and right difference quotients at zero are $(1,-1)$ and $(1,1)$, so the vector derivative does not exist there.

items.title: Two paths can have the same trace and endpoints but different lengths: one traverses $[0,1]$ once and another traverses it forward, backward, and forward
items.strategy: Use the identity path on $[0,1]$ and a three-piece affine path taking the successive values $0,1,0,1$. Both have trace $[0,1]$ and endpoints $0,1$. The polygonal-path formula gives lengths one and three, showing that length belongs to the parametrized path rather than its point set.

items.title: Sawtooth paths converge uniformly to a line segment while every sawtooth has length $\sqrt2$ and the limit has length $1$
items.strategy: On the uniform $n$-partition of $[0,1]$, join successive points whose horizontal separation is $1/n$ and whose vertical coordinates alternate between $0$ and $1/n$. The vertical sup norm is at most $1/n$, so the paths converge uniformly to $(t,0)$. Each of the $n$ affine edges has length $\sqrt2/n$, while the limit segment has length one.

items.title: The graph path $t\mapsto(t,c(t))$ of the Cantor function is rectifiable although its second coordinate is not absolutely continuous
items.strategy: The identity coordinate has variation one and the continuous nondecreasing Cantor function has variation one but is not absolutely continuous. The componentwise BV theorem makes the graph path rectifiable and bounds its length between its endpoint distance and two. Projection to the second coordinate shows that an absolutely continuous vector path would make $c$ absolutely continuous, giving the contradiction.
